To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
elevated carbon dioxide increased the biomass response of barley yellow dwarf virus‐infected plants, but did not alter the biomass response of healthy plants.
elevated CO2 increases the severity of disease and alters the plant's response to infection.
the response of plants infected with BYDV to elevated CO2 was different from the response of healthy plants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of CO2 and disease on plants.
the effects of elevated CO2 on the interaction between a host plant and a virus, which is a common pathogen in grasslands and cereal crops.
the effect of elevated CO2 on plant–pathogen interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the response of oat to elevated CO2 is altered by BYDV infection.
the effect of CO2 enrichment on the host plant is dependent upon the presence or absence of a pathogen, and the effect of the pathogen on the host is dependent upon the level of CO2.
the effect of BYDV infection on the response of A. sativa to CO2 was to increase the magnitude of the response to CO2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CO2 enrichment increased plant productivity and water-use efficiency, but these benefits were not equally distributed among all plants.
elevated CO2 can have a significant effect on the response of a plant to a viral infection.
CO2 enrichment increases disease severity, which may have important consequences for the response of ecosystems to elevated CO2.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of pathogens on plant growth are not constant and can change with environmental conditions.
pathogens can alter the response to CO2 of the plants they infect, and thus may play a role in the response of ecosystems to global change.
disease can alter the way plants respond to CO2 enrichment, and that the response may depend on the nature of the disease and the host plant.
